extracted.intended_audience: attorneys, parties, and representatives in Trademark Trial and Appeal Board (TTAB) inter partes proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on asserting and defending discovery requests, motions to compel, sanctions, and the Board’s standard and court-ordered protective orders in TTAB inter partes proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assertion of objections and motions to test sufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The rules provide for the assertion of objections to discovery requests believed to be improper, and a means (motion to compel for depositions/interrogatories/requests for production; motion to test sufficiency for requests for admission) for testing the sufficiency of those objections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a party believes a discovery request is improper it should assert specific objections; use the designated motion procedures to challenge sufficiency rather than bypassing those procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver for failure to respond absent excusable neglect
rubrics_metrics.description: A party which fails to respond to discovery requests during the time allowed and which cannot show its failure was the result of excusable neglect may be found, on motion to compel, to have forfeited its right to object to the discovery requests on their merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timely responses are critical; if you miss deadlines you risk forfeiting objections on the merits unless you can show excusable neglect. See TBMP § 407.01 for related guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merits objections vs confidentiality/privilege objections
rubrics_metrics.description: Objections going to the merits include challenges that a request is overly broad, unduly vague or ambiguous, burdensome and oppressive, seeks non-discoverable information on expert witnesses, or is not calculated to lead to admissible evidence. By contrast, claims of trade secret, business-sensitive/confidential information, attorney-client privilege, or attorney work product do not go to the merits but to characteristics of the responsive information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate objections carefully: confidentiality/privilege objections are treated differently and generally are not considered waived even if other merits objections are forfeited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality objections generally preserved
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board generally is not inclined to hold a party to have waived the right to make objections based on confidentiality, privilege, or work product, even where the party is otherwise held to have waived its right to make objections to the merits of discovery requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of the Board’s standard protective order, parties should still assert confidentiality/privilege when appropriate; these objections are treated more favorably than pure merits objections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Failure to serve initial disclosures as ground to object
rubrics_metrics.description: For proceedings commenced on or after November 1, 2007, failure to serve initial disclosures constitutes a proper ground for objection to discovery requests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you believe the propounding party failed to serve initial disclosures and therefore you need not respond, you have a duty to object on that basis. However, see notes that mistaken beliefs do not excuse failure to respond substantively.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate response method to discovery rather than filing motions
rubrics_metrics.description: It is generally inappropriate to respond to a request for discovery by filing a motion attacking it (e.g., motion to strike, suppress, or for protective order); ordinarily the party should provide the information it believes proper and state objections to the remainder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only in limited circumstances (clear harassment, unreasonable number of requests, or not real party in interest) should a motion for protective order or other attack be filed instead of serving responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objection to excessive interrogatories must be a timely general objection
rubrics_metrics.description: If a responding party believes the number of interrogatories exceeds the limit specified in 37 CFR § 2.120(d)(1), the responding party must, within the time for (and instead of) serving answers and specific objections, serve a general objection on the ground of their excessive number; a motion for protective order is not the proper method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serve the specific general objection timely rather than seeking protection by motion; see TBMP § 405.03(e) for remedies.

rubrics_metrics.name: When to file motions to quash or for protective order against depositions
rubrics_metrics.description: A party on which a notice of deposition was served may file a motion to quash the notice of deposition or a motion for a protective order if the notice is insufficient, vague, would cause the propounding party to exceed permitted depositions, or would result in a deposition being taken outside the discovery period.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use motion practice when the deposition notice violates procedural limits or scheduling; see TBMP §§ 521 and 526.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions to compel initial and expert disclosures — timing and prerequisites
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial disclosures must comply with Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(1)(A) and (E) and expert disclosures with Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(a)(2). A motion to compel initial disclosures or expert testimony disclosures must be filed prior to the close of the discovery period, and filing a motion to compel is a prerequisite to a motion for sanctions for failure to make or for insufficient disclosures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To seek sanctions under 37 CFR § 2.120(g)(1) or (g)(2), first move to compel and obtain an order; motions to compel are necessary before sanctions motions in most circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy by motion to compel for interrogatories and production
rubrics_metrics.description: If any party fails to answer any interrogatory or fails to produce documents for inspection and copying, the party seeking discovery may file a motion for an order to compel an answer or production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not seek immediate entry of sanctions for no response unless the responding party has expressly informed the inquiring party that no response will be made. See TBMP § 523 for practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for failure to respond to requests for admission
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party fails to file a timely response to requests for admission, the requests will stand admitted unless the failure resulted from excusable neglect or unless a motion to withdraw or amend the admissions is filed under Fed. R. Civ. P. 36(b) and granted by the Board.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A propounding party dissatisfied with an answer or objection may file a motion to determine sufficiency; the Board may order admission or that an amended answer be served. If a matter is admitted or denied, that constitutes a proper response even if objections are included.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery deposition remedies and limits (30(b)(6), non-party witnesses)
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party fails to designate a person under Fed. R. Civ. P. 30(b)(6) or fails to attend or answer at a discovery deposition, the propounding party may file a motion to compel. The Board lacks jurisdiction to compel a non-party witness; subpoenas must be enforced in the issuing federal district court under 35 U.S.C. § 24.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: During depositions objections may be stated but questions normally should be answered subject to objection. If a witness refuses to answer and the deposition is under subpoena, the deposing party may adjourn and seek a district court order to compel; otherwise complete the deposition and move to compel with the Board.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctions available for failure to provide disclosures or discovery
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may impose a variety of sanctions, pursuant to 37 CFR § 2.120(g) and Fed. R. Civ. P. 37(b)(2), including striking pleadings, refusing to allow support or opposition for claims/defenses, drawing adverse inferences, prohibiting introduction of designated matters in evidence, and entering judgment against the disobedient party; the Board will not hold contempt or award expenses including attorneys' fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions must be appropriate to the misconduct; consult TBMP § 527.01 for further information and the limitations on awards of fees and contempt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board’s standard protective order — automatic applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board’s standard protective order is applicable during disclosure, discovery and at trial in all opposition, cancellation, interference and concurrent use registration proceedings, unless parties, by stipulation approved by the Board, agree to an alternative order, or a motion to use an alternative order is granted by the Board. For inter partes proceedings pending or commenced on or after August 31, 2007, it is automatically in place.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties are notified that the standard order applies; the standard protective order is available on the USPTO website. It is not necessary to sign copies for it to take effect, though parties may do so.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classes of protected information under the standard protective order
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board’s standard protective order provides three tiers of protected information: Confidential (material shielded from public access), Highly Confidential (shielded and subject to agreed restrictions on access even as to parties/attorneys), and Trade Secret/Commercially Sensitive (shielded from public access and restricted from party access; available to outside counsel and, subject to terms, to independent experts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Access rules differ by tier: parties and their attorneys have access to confidential/highly confidential; outside counsel (but not in-house counsel) have access to trade secret materials; independent experts/non-party witnesses may be granted access if they sign acknowledgements and meet conditions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Information not eligible for protection
rubrics_metrics.description: Information may not be designated as protected if it (a) is or becomes public knowledge other than through a violation of the order; (b) is acquired by a non-designating party from a third party lawfully possessing it; (c) was lawfully possessed by a non-designating party prior to discovery with written evidence; (d) is disclosed by a non-designating party legally compelled to disclose; or (e) is disclosed by a non-designating party with approval of the designating party.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to designate universally-public or lawfully-obtained information as protected; such designations will be invalid.

rubrics_metrics.name: Access rules and obligations for protected information
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties and their attorneys shall have access to confidential or highly confidential information subject to any agreed exceptions. Outside counsel, but not in-house counsel, shall have access to trade secret/commercially sensitive information. Independent experts, consultants, non-party witnesses and others may be given access under conditions (including signing acknowledgements).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The burden is on the party seeking protection to designate appropriately. Failure to designate or redact confidential portions when filing or responding may waive confidentiality. Parties must meaningfully limit designations to information that warrants the level of protection claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parties cannot withhold discoverable information solely on confidentiality grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties cannot withhold properly discoverable information on the basis of confidentiality since the Board’s standard protective order automatically applies; where a party refuses to provide discoverable information on confidentiality grounds, the Board may order production consistent with the protective order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the standard protective order to protect information rather than refusing production; if special protection is needed, seek modification or separate protective order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motions for protective order under 37 CFR § 2.120(f) — scope and burden
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon motion by a party obligated to make disclosures or from whom discovery is sought, and for good cause, the Board may make any order justice requires to protect a party from annoyance, embarrassment, oppression, or undue burden or expense, including types of orders in clauses (A)–(H) of Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(c). To establish good cause, the movant must submit 'a particular and specific demonstration of fact' rather than conclusory statements; the movant bears the burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board may impose terms short of denying discovery; if a motion for protective order is denied, the Board may order discovery on just terms. The standard protective order does not preclude moving for additional protection where the standard order is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Filing discovery materials with the Board — general rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Initial and expert disclosures, and supplemental discovery responses, like all discovery, should not be filed with the Board except under circumstances specified in 37 CFR § 2.120(j)(8); rebuttal disclosures are not a means for filing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not routinely file discovery materials with the Board; to consider discovery materials on summary judgment, they must be submitted with the motion or brief as permitted. Use notices of reliance or other authorized mechanisms when introducing discovery materials into the record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of produced documents and authenticity mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents produced in response to interrogatories or other discovery may be made of record by notice of reliance where authenticity is established (e.g., by adversary’s admission, request for admission, or other procedural mechanisms).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a responding party avails itself of Fed. R. Civ. P. 33(d) and admits produced documents are true and correct copies, those documents may be introduced by notice of reliance. Check relevant precedents (e.g., Kohler Co. v. Baldwin Hardware Corp.) for examples.
